96: /** Widest the right panel may be while keeping the manuscript usable. */

100: /**
101:  * Below this the rails stop being furniture and start being the whole screen,
102:  * so they are undocked rather than squeezed. Matches Tailwind's `sm`, which is
103:  * where the toolbar also switches to a single scrolling row.
104:  */
105: const NARROW_VIEWPORT = 640;

107: function maxRightPanelWidth(leftSidebarOpen: boolean): number {
108:   const reserved =
109:     (leftSidebarOpen ? LEFT_SIDEBAR_WIDTH : 0) + MIN_EDITOR_WIDTH;
110:   // The 260px floor is a minimum *useful* panel, not a promise there is room
111:   // for one: on a 390px phone it left the manuscript 122px wide. Callers must
112:   // check `fitsDockedPanel` before docking rather than trusting this number.
113:   return Math.max(260, Math.min(560, window.innerWidth - reserved));
114: }
115: 
116: /** Is there room to dock a rail without crushing the manuscript? */
117: function fitsDockedPanel(leftSidebarOpen: boolean): boolean {
118:   if (window.innerWidth < NARROW_VIEWPORT) return false;
119:   const reserved =
120:     (leftSidebarOpen ? LEFT_SIDEBAR_WIDTH : 0) + MIN_EDITOR_WIDTH;
121:   return window.innerWidth - reserved >= 260;
122: }

158: /* ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
159:  *  Editorial dateline — formatted like a print magazine masthead.
160:  *  e.g. "Vol. I · No. 117 · Sunday, the 26th of April, 2026"
161:  * ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
162: function editorialDateline(now = new Date()): string {
163:   const days = [
164:     "Sunday",
165:     "Monday",
166:     "Tuesday",
167:     "Wednesday",
168:     "Thursday",
169:     "Friday",
170:     "Saturday",
171:   ];
172:   const months = [
173:     "January",
174:     "February",
175:     "March",
176:     "April",
177:     "May",
178:     "June",
179:     "July",
180:     "August",
181:     "September",
182:     "October",
183:     "November",
184:     "December",
185:   ];
186:   const day = now.getDate();
187:   const ordinal = (n: number) => {
188:     const s = ["th", "st", "nd", "rd"];
189:     const v = n % 100;
190:     return n + (s[(v - 20) % 10] || s[v] || s[0]);
191:   };
192:   const start = new Date(now.getFullYear(), 0, 0);
193:   const diff = (now.getTime() - start.getTime()) / 86400000;
194:   const dayOfYear = Math.floor(diff);
195:   return `Vol. I · No. ${dayOfYear} · ${days[now.getDay()]}, the ${ordinal(day)} of ${months[now.getMonth()]}, ${now.getFullYear()}`;
196: }

The City Receives You

T he city receives you before you arrive. You feel it in the tilt of the light, the way shopkeepers arrange their windows, the particular silence of a side street at dusk. Every neighbourhood is a paragraph; every boulevard a long sentence winding toward some punctuation you cannot yet see.

To write about a place is to argue with it. The buildings resist metaphor. The traffic ignores your symbolism. And yet—if you sit still long enough—the city begins to dictate its own grammar. You become less an author than a stenographer, recording what was already there.

The Margin as Method

The best drafts are not composed in isolation. They are written in the margins of other books, in the pauses between conversations, in the white space that surrounds another person's argument. content.text:
The three static labels are now an 8-stop guided tour. What changed:

**`workspace-tour.tsx` (new)** — `WorkspaceTour` wraps the preview with:
- **Pulsing ✦ hotspots** over each region (dossier, folios, manuscript, cast, rubric + the three board tabs). Active hotspot fills with its accent color. Wide-screens only, so coordinates stay honest when rails are docked.
- **Reader card** below the preview showing "Stop N of 8 · Tag" + the note, with prev/next arrows and per-stop dots. It remounts per stop (`key={stop.id}`), replaying the rise transition — so cards visibly transition on every change.
- **Auto-advance** every 5s, pausing on hover/focus, disabled entirely under `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- **Two-way sync**: picking a hotspot drives the preview (the Folios stop opens the research notes, the Rubric stop switches the board tab…), and playing with the preview drives the cards — clicking any board tab, folio, or reopening the drawer jumps the card to the matching stop.

**Adding a card is one list entry.** Everything — hotspot, dots, preview state, card copy — derives from the exported `TOUR_STOPS` array at the top of the file. To explain a new part of the interface, append `{ id, tag, note, accent, tab, folioId, drawer, panel, hotspot: {x, y} }` and you're done.

**Supporting changes:**
- `workspace-preview.tsx` — gained controlled props (`tab`, `folioId`, `drawer`, `panel` + `onXChange$` callbacks) so the tour can drive it; uncontrolled behavior (used by the existing 7 stories and anywhere else) is untouched.
- `landing-page.tsx` — the old `annotations` array and its floating/mobile lists are replaced by `<WorkspaceTour />`; dead `.landing-annotation` CSS removed, hotspot/dot/step styles added to `global.css` with reduced-motion handling.
- `workspace-tour.stories.tsx` (new) — Default, RubricStop, FoliosStop, plus an `initialStopId` select control.

content.text:
Back to the overlay style — no more scrolling. The description now floats over the room itself:

**Reader slip, pinned to the hotspot.** Each stop's card renders inside the preview frame, anchored to its ✦ marker (above or below it), so the explanation is read exactly where the eye already is. Clicking hotspots, dots, arrows, or the preview's own tabs/folios all swap the slip in place — everything happens in one viewport.

Details:
- **Per-stop `placement`** (`"above"` / `"below"`) on each `TOUR_STOPS` entry, chosen so the slip doesn't cover the element it describes — e.g. the Cast slip hangs above the persona cards, the Manuscript slip below the drop cap, the tab-row stops below the tab strip. Tune it per stop by flipping one field.
- **Transition preserved**: the slip remounts per stop (`key={stop.id}`) replaying the rise entrance. It positions with the `translate` CSS property rather than `transform`, so the entrance animation can't fight the centering.
- **Step controls live in the slip**: compact ← / 8 dots / → row, so navigation never leaves the overlay either.
- **Small screens**: hotspots stay hidden and the slip docks as a bottom sheet inside the frame (`left: 50%`, bottom-anchored), so it can't overflow or cover the whole preview.
- Auto-advance, hover/focus pause, reduced-motion handling, and two-way preview sync all work as before.

Jev (`jev-1.13.0`, via the direct TypeSafe path, ~14k input tokens) has judged the tour. One caveat up front: the judgement contract returns structured scores only — despite asking, no prose rationale came back (129 output tokens, numbers alone). Here's the verdict:

| Area | Score /4 | Read |
|---|---|---|
| Visual styling | **3.65** (66% exceptional) | Clear strength — the broadsheet language carries it |
| Interface design | **3.19** (74% strong) | Solid, not exceptional |
| Code quality | **2.90** (73% strong, but 16% of mass at adequate-or-worse) | Lowest — worth a look |
| Biggest risk | **hotspot-discoverability** (37%) | …but confidence only 0.22, with auto-advance-timing (33%) and slip-covers-content (26%) right behind — effectively a three-way tie |

What I take from that:
- **Styling: ship it.** Nothing to fix.
- **Interface: the risk split is the finding.** No single dominant flaw; instead three moderate ones. Two are already mitigated by design (the slip now carries its own dots/arrows, so discovery doesn't depend on noticing hotspots; per-stop placement + bottom-sheet keep content visible). The third — timing fighting reading — was the cheapest to address, so I bumped auto-advance 5s → 6s.
- **Code quality at 2.9** with that 16% weak-tail is the one I'd actually probe next. Candidates from my own reading: the `goTo` interval reading `stopIndex.value` at fire time (correct, but subtle), and the controlled/uncontrolled prop split in the preview doubling state paths. If you want, I can put a second, narrower Jev question set on just those two spots — or hunting the weak-tail with a focused re-read myself.

Want me to chase the code-quality tail, or leave the tour here?

license: MIT
description: >
  Build AI-powered software with TypeSafe: small units of AI intelligence you
  can use like programming primitives. Its System One models, including Jev,
  turn natural language and application state into typed judgments and

# Build with TypeSafe

TypeSafe makes units of AI intelligence usable like programming primitives: small
judgments you can compose into larger capabilities. Its **System One models** return
fast, focused judgments that software can consume directly. **Jev** is TypeSafe's
flagship and first System One model. It understands natural language and returns
typed answers and probabilities rather
than generating text or reasoning explanations. Code owns the workflow; the model
supplies programmable common sense where ordinary code needs semantic understanding.

## Read the live docs

**The live TypeSafe docs are the source of truth. Read them as part of the task.**
This skill gives direction; the docs carry current concepts, prompting guidance,
API contracts, SDK usage, models, limits, and worked examples.

- Start with the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt) to discover
  relevant pages and cookbooks. Use targeted reads rather than loading the entire site.
- Mintlify serves Markdown by appending `.md` to a page path, for example
  [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md).
  Follow links from the index; convert extensionless documentation page links to
  `.md` when useful. Resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Before writing an integration, read the current API or chosen SDK page and the
  question guidance relevant to the design. For a new workflow, also inspect the
  closest cookbook: it often shows a better decomposition than a generic classifier.
- If the index is unavailable, use the direct links below or the site's navigation.
  If Markdown fetching fails, try the normal page. If live access is unavailable,
  use available local docs or installed SDK types, state that limitation, and avoid
  inventing version-dependent details.

| Task | Start here; follow the relevant details |
| --- | --- |
| Understand the programming model | [System One](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one.md), [building guide](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md) |
| Explore what to build | [Use-case map](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/use-case-map.md), then relevant cookbooks from the index |
| Prepare inputs and questions | [State](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state.md), [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives.md), then the chosen primitive's page |
| Decide how to handle uncertainty | [Confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence.md) |
| Write API code | [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/api.md), [Python SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/python.md), or [JavaScript SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/javascript.md) |
| Update an older integration | [Migration guide](https://docs.typesafe.ai/migrating-to-v1.md) and the installed SDK's current reference |

## Find the useful shape

Start from the behavior the user wants: what will the application show, select,
change, or hand off? Work backward to the judgments it needs. Keep known rules,
calculations, exact lookups, and execution in code. Preserve the user's chosen stack
and scope; add TypeSafe where semantic understanding helps.

When brainstorming or choosing an architecture, consider more than classification.
The patterns below are starting points: combine primitives around the user's goal,
including ideas that do not fit an established recipe.

- **Route and fill known arguments.** A request can select a handler and its typed
  parameters. Ask useful branch-specific questions up front and consume only the
  relevant answers. Explore [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md)
  and [speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Find candidate values or source spans in code,
  use a judgment to select the intended one, then copy or normalize it. Code can
  also assemble source text into a formatted document or reading guide. Explore
  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md)
  and [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates, compare their relevance to a
  query, and select useful context. Explore [reranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md)
  and [hierarchical classification](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/hierarchical_classification.md).
- **Turn judgments into reusable data.** Score dimensions once, then let code or
  user controls change weights, thresholds, rankings, and views. With labeled
  outcomes, those signals can become classical ML features. Explore
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check specific claims or fields against their evidence;
  send uncertain or failing cases to a person or reasoning model. Explore
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).
- **Respond to changing state.** Code can retain goals and observations while fresh
  judgments guide the next bounded step. Keep inferred state distinct from observed
  facts, and check freshness before applying a result to a changed situation.

For open-ended requests, offer the few directions that best serve the user's goal
and recommend a starting point. For a concrete request, choose the relevant pattern
and build; a brainstorm is not a mandatory detour.

## Design the judgments

Choose by what the answer means, then read the relevant primitive page:

| Need | Primitive | Important distinction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One of a defined set | [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md) | Picks one option; its distribution compares competing options |
| Whether a condition holds | [Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul.md) | Probability of yes; no separate confidence; use one per label when several may apply |
| Degree along a described dimension | [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md) | Probability-weighted position on ordered levels; use comparable per-item Scores for graded ranking |

Give each question enough relevant **state** to answer: source text, identities,
relationships, policies, and current facts. Prefer named JSON fields when context
has several parts. Put the judgment in **instructions** and define its possible
answers in **criteria**. Question IDs are for code and are not sent to the model;
include complete meaning in the question. Reference nested state with backticked
paths such as `ticket.messages[0].text`.

Ask one narrow, coherent judgment per question. Split independently useful dimensions,
without destroying the relationship being judged. A bounded action selection or
contextual interpretation is valid; atomic does not mean literal fact extraction
or a one-sentence limit. Strings work for simple questions. Use structured objects
or arrays when definitions, contrasts, exclusions, or examples clarify instructions
or criteria. Score levels must describe concrete situations and stand on their own.

Keep the needed answers available. Include a no-match outcome when nothing may fit;
use a separate presence judgment when it is independently useful. For source-value
selection, check candidate coverage: the model cannot choose an omitted value.

## Compose and verify

**Ask independent questions over the same state together**, including useful
speculative questions. They run in parallel and cannot see one another's answers.
State each speculative premise explicitly; code consumes the applicable answers.
A second request is warranted when an earlier answer is needed to fetch evidence,
construct new state, or determine the next options. Extra questions still use tokens;
measure actual request budgets, cost, and end-to-end latency.

Use probabilities and confidence to guide behavior, with thresholds evaluated on
the user's data and consequences. Choice/Score confidence summarizes distribution
concentration, not overall workflow correctness or permission to act. A Noul near
0.5 means similar probability for yes and no, not medium intensity. Several
acceptable alternatives can also spread probability; low confidence need not
invalidate a harmless preference choice. Ignore uncertainty on unused branches.

Keep policy explicit and raw judgments reusable. Weighted scores suit compensating
preferences; an “any serious violation” rule needs separate conditions. Changing a
weight or display filter need not rerun inference when evidence and question meanings
are unchanged. Typed output guarantees the interface, not truth. System One models
are trained for calibrated decisions; validate their performance in the target domain.

Test representative cases and the resulting application behavior. For failures,
inspect the exact state, questions, candidates, answers, composition, and observed
outcome. Separate missing evidence, model errors, code errors, and service failures.
Treat cookbook thresholds and demo results as examples to evaluate, not universal
rules or permanent model limitations. Keep API credentials server-side in web apps.

# Confidence

> How TypeSafe reports certainty, how it differs from probability, and how to use it to control system behavior.

All Score and Choice answers from TypeSafe include a `probabilities` property representing the probability distribution across the options (for Choice) or levels (for Score). The *shape* of that distribution is what tells you how certain the model is: concentrated on one outcome means a confident answer, spread out means an uncertain one.

The answer's `confidence` property collapses that shape into a single number from 0 to 1, so you can threshold on it without doing the math yourself. (Noul answers don't carry one.)

## Confidence is derived from the probabilities

`confidence` is a statistic computed from the probability distribution the answer already gives you. TypeSafe computes it for you and returns it on every Choice and Score answer, so the common case needs no extra work on your side.

<Note>
  **A solid default:** We provide `confidence` as a convenient measure that fits most use-cases, but you are never locked into our definition. Depending on what you are evaluating, a different measure may serve you better, which is exactly why we give you the full `probabilities` in the response. The pros and cons of different computations is a specialized topic that we'll keep to a separate cookbook rather than this page, and will add the link here when we do!
</Note>

For a [Choice](/primitives/choice), the distribution is `probabilities` across your options. For a [Score](/primitives/score), it is the distribution across your levels. In both cases a flatter distribution means lower confidence: low confidence on a Choice often means none of the options are a clear winner over the others, and low confidence on a Score often means the levels are ambiguous, multi-dimensional, or the state doesn't contain enough to go on.

## "I don't know" is a useful signal

If an intelligent system, whether human or machine, cannot express honest uncertainty, the system cannot be trusted.

Confidence gives you a built-in mechanism for the model to say "I'm not sure about this one." This lets your code implement different behavior for different levels of certainty, which is the foundation for building systems you can actually rely on.

## Three paths for using confidence in your code

A useful starting pattern is to divide confidence into three ranges, each producing a different system behavior:

**High confidence:** Act automatically. The model has a clear read and you can proceed without human involvement.

**Medium confidence:** Proceed with caution. The model has a reasonable answer but is not certain. Depending on context, you might ask the user to confirm, flag for review, or gather more information before acting.

**Low confidence:** Do not act. Route to a human, request clarification, or fall back to a different system. The model is telling you it does not have enough information or the question is not a good fit.

Where you draw those boundaries depends on the stakes.

## Thresholds scale with risk

A confidence threshold is not one number. Different actions within the same system should be gated at different levels depending on the consequences of getting it wrong.

```python theme={null}
response = client.system_one(
    state=user_message,
    questions={
        "action": Choice(
            instructions="What is the user trying to do?",
            criteria={
                "check_balance": "View account balance",
                "approve_transfer": "Approve the pending withdrawal request",
                "support": "Get help with an issue",
            },
        ),
    },
)

action = response.answers["action"]
confidence = action.confidence

if confidence < 0.5:
    # Model is genuinely unsure. Don't guess.
    route_to_human(user_message)

elif action.choice == "check_balance":
    # Low stakes. Showing the wrong screen is recoverable.
    show_balance(account_id)

elif action.choice == "approve_transfer":
    if confidence > 0.9:
        # High stakes, high confidence. Proceed with confirmation.
        confirm_then_execute(account_id)
    else:
        # High stakes, moderate confidence. Verify first.
        ask_user_to_confirm(account_id)
```

The 0.5 confidence floor catches anything the model reports as genuinely uncertain. Above that, the threshold for acting without confirmation is higher for a destructive operation than for a read-only one. Your code encodes the risk tolerance.

<Note>
  The correct threshold values depend on your domain and the performance of the model for your use case. Start with conservative thresholds, test with your own data, and adjust as you observe results.
</Note>

Skill installed and applied. Summary of the whole exercise:

**Installed**: `typesafe-ai` skill at project level (`.agents/skills/typesafe-ai/`, tracked in `skills-lock.json`). Note: my live skill registry is session-static so I worked from the skill file + live docs directly, which is what the skill instructs anyway.

**Used it on the tour.** Reading the live docs changed the evaluation: my first Jev run used bare-adjective levels (`poor…exceptional`), which the Score doc explicitly warns give the model nothing to match against. I rewrote the questions per the skill — one dimension each, situational levels — and re-ran. Final verdict (`jev-1.13.0`, 0–3 scales):

| Question | Score | Confidence | Read |
|---|---|---|---|
| visual craft | **2.62** (63% top level) | 0.62 | Strength, matches round 1 |
| interface clarity | **2.33** (56% L2, 39% L3) | 0.56 | Strong lean, some visitors may still miss regions |
| code correctness | **2.35** (split L2/L3) | 0.35 | No red flags, but low confidence = genuine spread, don't over-read it |
| accessibility | **2.11** (19% on "operable but missing something") | 0.48 | Weakest — acted on it |
| biggest risk | hotspot-discoverability (36%) | 0.21 | Flat three-way tie again — i.e. no single dominant flaw |

**Fix applied from the verdict**: added `aria-live="polite"` to the reader slip, so auto-advance announces stop changes to screen readers (the likely gap behind that 19% mass). tsc/prettier clean, 131 stories, no index errors. I also bumped auto-advance to 6s earlier against the timing risk.

Residuals I'm deliberately leaving: dots use tab roles without arrow-key roving (plain Tab/Enter works), and hotspots stay desktop-only by design (dots + arrows carry mobile). Per the skill's confidence guidance, the flat risk distribution means "don't act on it alone" — so no redesign from that question.
think of other places to use it for our code quality, look for what we ask for in prompts, be  creative, see where we can identify problems!
Mapping where the codebase already leans on LLM prompts and judgments, then I'll get creative from there.

Design creative TypeSafe insertion points (questions, state, primitives)
Run a demo Jev judgement that identifies a real problem

1: /**
2:  * TypeSafe "System One" (Jev) — typed questions and answers.
3:  *
4:  * Jev does not generate text. It answers a fixed set of questions about some
5:  * state, and returns a calibrated probability distribution for each one. That
6:  * is the whole surface: three question kinds, three answer shapes.
7:  *
8:  *   Noul    probability of yes, 0..1
9:  *   Choice  pick one option, plus the probability of every option
10:  *   Score   ordered levels, returning a probability-weighted value
11:  *
12:  * This module is transport-free on purpose. It builds requests and reads
13:  * answers; `convex/systemOne.ts` is the only place that holds the API key and
14:  * talks to the network, because the key must never reach the browser bundle.
15:  *
16:  * Costs, measured against the live API rather than quoted from the docs: the
17:  * full 11-criterion rubric spine batched into one request took 378 ms and
18:  * 1,401 input tokens — $0.0000588, or roughly 17,000 rubric passes per dollar.
19:  * Output tokens are free. This is cheap enough to run on a typing pause.
20:  */
21: 
22: /* ── Questions ─────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
23: 
24: /** Probability that the answer is yes. */
25: export interface NoulQuestion {
26:   type: "noul";
27:   instructions: string;
28: }
29: 
30: /** Pick exactly one of `criteria`. */
31: export interface ChoiceQuestion {
32:   type: "choice";
33:   instructions: string;
34:   criteria: string[];
35: }
36: 
37: /**
38:  * Ordered levels, worst first. The answer is a probability-weighted value
39:  * across them, so it can land between two levels.
40:  */
41: export interface ScoreQuestion {
42:   type: "score";
43:   instructions: string;
44:   criteria: string[];
45: }
46: 
47: export type SystemOneQuestion = NoulQuestion | ChoiceQuestion | ScoreQuestion;
48: 
49: /**
50:  * One request. Independent questions over the same `state` run in parallel
51:  * and barely change latency, so batch aggressively — but they cannot see each
52:  * other's answers. A second round-trip is only justified when an answer is
53:  * needed to *fetch* new evidence.
54:  *
55:  * Budget: 64k context per request, of which 32k is for `state`.
56:  */
57: export interface SystemOneRequest {
58:   model?: string;
59:   state: Record<string, unknown>;
60:   questions: Record<string, SystemOneQuestion>;
61: }
62: 
63: /* ── Answers ───────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
64: 
65: export interface NoulAnswer {
66:   type: "noul";
67:   /** 0 (no) to 1 (yes). */
68:   noul: number;
69: }
70: 
71: export interface ChoiceAnswer {
72:   type: "choice";
73:   /** The highest-probability option. */
74:   choice: string;
75:   /** Every option mapped to its probability; sums to 1. */
76:   probabilities: Record<string, number>;
77:   confidence: number;
78: }
79: 
80: export interface ScoreAnswer {
81:   type: "score";
82:   /** Probability-weighted across levels; can land between them. */
83:   score: number;
84:   /** Level index (as a string key) back to its description. */
85:   legend: Record<string, string>;
86:   /** Level index to probability; sums to 1. */
87:   probabilities: Record<string, number>;
88:   confidence: number;
89: }
90: 
91: export type SystemOneAnswer = NoulAnswer | ChoiceAnswer | ScoreAnswer;
92: 
93: export interface SystemOneUsage {
94:   input_tokens: number;
95:   output_tokens: number;
96: }
97: 
98: export interface SystemOneResponse {
99:   model: string;
100:   answers: Record<string, SystemOneAnswer>;
101:   usage: SystemOneUsage;
102: }
103: 
104: /** Input tokens only — output is not billed. */
105: export const USD_PER_INPUT_TOKEN = 0.042 / 1_000_000;
106: 
107: export function estimateCost(usage: SystemOneUsage): number {
108:   return usage.input_tokens * USD_PER_INPUT_TOKEN;
109: }
110: 
111: /* ── Builders ──────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
112: 
113: export function noul(instructions: string): NoulQuestion {
114:   return { type: "noul", instructions };
115: }
116: 
117: export function choice(
118:   instructions: string,
119:   criteria: string[],
120: ): ChoiceQuestion {
121:   return { type: "choice", instructions, criteria };
122: }
123: 
124: /** `criteria` must be ordered worst-to-best; the index is the level. */
125: export function score(instructions: string, criteria: string[]): ScoreQuestion {
126:   return { type: "score", instructions, criteria };
127: }
128: 
129: /* ── Reading answers ───────────────────────────────────────────── */
130: 
131: export function isNoul(a: SystemOneAnswer | undefined): a is NoulAnswer {
132:   return a?.type === "noul";
133: }
134: 
135: export function isChoice(a: SystemOneAnswer | undefined): a is ChoiceAnswer {
136:   return a?.type === "choice";
137: }
138: 
139: export function isScore(a: SystemOneAnswer | undefined): a is ScoreAnswer {
140:   return a?.type === "score";
141: }
142: 
143: /**
144:  * Whether a Score's distribution is bimodal — mass at both ends with a trough
145:  * in the middle, which is exactly where the weighted mean lands.
146:  *
147:  * This is not hypothetical. A measured answer came back `score: 1.43`,
148:  * `confidence: 0.14`, `probabilities: {0: 0.21, 1: 0.16, 2: 0.63}`: the scalar
149:  * points at the level the model assigned the *least* mass to. Any threshold on
150:  * the scalar alone would have been wrong. Callers below their confidence floor
151:  * should branch on the distribution or decline to show a grade at all.
152:  */
153: export function isBimodal(answer: ScoreAnswer): boolean {
154:   const levels = Object.keys(answer.probabilities)
155:     .map(Number)
156:     .sort((a, b) => a - b);
157:   if (levels.length < 3) return false;
158: 
159:   const nearest = Math.round(answer.score);
160:   const pAtMean = answer.probabilities[String(nearest)] ?? 0;
161:   const peak = Math.max(...Object.values(answer.probabilities));
162: 
163:   // The mean sits in a trough: some level is at least twice as likely as the
164:   // one the mean actually names.
165:   return peak > pAtMean * 2;
166: }
167: 
168: /**
169:  * The level the model gave the most mass to, which is not always the level
170:  * nearest `score`. Use this when `isBimodal` is true and you still must pick.
171:  */
172: export function modalLevel(answer: ScoreAnswer): number {
173:   let best = 0;
174:   let bestP = -1;
175:   for (const [level, p] of Object.entries(answer.probabilities)) {
176:     if (p > bestP) {
177:       bestP = p;
178:       best = Number(level);
179:     }
180:   }
181:   return best;
182: }
183: 
184: /**
185:  * Rescale a Score onto 0..max (Twyne's rubric is 0–10) using the number of
186:  * levels the question declared, not a hardcoded assumption.
187:  */
188: export function scoreOutOf(answer: ScoreAnswer, max: number): number {
189:   const levels = Object.keys(answer.legend).length;
190:   if (levels < 2) return 0;
191:   return (answer.score / (levels - 1)) * max;
192: }
193: 
194: /* ── Confidence semantics ──────────────────────────────────────── */
195: 
196: /**
197:  * What `confidence` does and does not mean, kept here so call sites cannot
198:  * quietly reinvent it:
199:  *
200:  * - For a Noul there is no confidence field at all. A Noul near 0.5 means
201:  *   *equally likely yes or no* — it does not mean "medium intensity". Reading
202:  *   a Noul as a magnitude is the most common way to misuse this API.
203:  * - For Choice and Score, confidence measures how concentrated the probability
204:  *   distribution is. It is **not** a correctness estimate and **not**
205:  *   permission to act. Low confidence often just means several answers are
206:  *   equally fine.
207:  *
208:  * Empirically this tracks objectivity, which is the useful part: on a
209:  * deliberately bad draft, `integrity` scored 0.01 at confidence 0.99 while the
210:  * genuinely subjective `targetFit` scored 2.38 at confidence 0.43. That makes
211:  * confidence a good trigger for escalating to a frontier model, and a bad
212:  * trigger for taking an action on the user's behalf.
213:  */
214: export function confidenceOf(answer: SystemOneAnswer): number | null {
215:   return isNoul(answer) ? null : answer.confidence;
216: }

1: /**
2:  * Grading persona notes before the writer ever sees them.
3:  *
4:  * This inverts the usual ladder. Everywhere else the cheap engine answers
5:  * first and the expensive one is the escalation; here the expensive engine
6:  * answers and the cheap one decides whether the answer was any good. That
7:  * works because the two failures are asymmetric: a frontier model writing
8:  * vague, unactionable advice is common, and *recognising* vague advice is easy
9:  * — much easier than producing good advice in the first place.
10:  *
11:  * At ~$0.00006 per batched pass, gating every note costs less than the note
12:  * did by three orders of magnitude, so the gate is affordable even when it
13:  * rejects and forces a rewrite.
14:  *
15:  * The composition rule is deliberately not a weighted mean. There are three
16:  * classes, and they compose differently on purpose:
17:  *
18:  *   quality      averages   helpful / actionable / servesGoal
19:  *   constraints  veto       the brief's non-negotiables
20:  *   adherence    routes     does this read as the editor who signed it
21:  *
22:  * A note can be the most helpful, most actionable thing the room has ever
23:  * produced and still be unusable because the writer said "no second person"
24:  * and it rewrites a line into second person. Averaging those together would
25:  * let helpfulness buy off a constraint the writer declared non-negotiable,
26:  * which is exactly backwards.
27:  *
28:  * Adherence is the third case and it is neither of the first two. Averaging it
29:  * in would promote a beautifully in-voice note that says nothing, and sink an
30:  * off-voice note that sees something nobody else saw. Vetoing on it would
31:  * throw away real advice to protect a costume. So it never touches `pass` and
32:  * never touches `overall`; it decides *which rewrite to ask for*. The
33:  * mechanical guarantee is that `adherence` is not a member of
34:  * `NOTE_DIMENSIONS`, which is the only thing `overall` averages over.

content.text:
Sweep done — Jev audited our prompts and our Jev questions, and found real problems. Then the creative part: where else to use it.

## What Jev identified (measured, `jev-1.13.0`)

**Prompt audit** (state: the 5 judge prompt pairs):
- **`output_fragility` Noul = 0.88** — the strongest finding. Every judge demands JSON-only with a free-text `rationale` and no escaping rule; one unescaped quote kills the parse. I verified the failure mode in code: `ai-client.ts` strips fences → `JSON.parse` → silent `null` on failure. A judge can die on a quotation mark and the feature just degrades.
- **`self_contradiction` = 0.71** — 10-point scales with 2–4 anchors. Sufficiency anchors only 1 and 10 ("most first drafts land 3-6" — i.e. the entire middle is vibes). Target-fit demands blindness to craft while judging audience fit.
- **`weakest_prompt` = sufficiency (0.66)**, dossier-check runner-up (0.28). Caveat: my state accidentally omitted `sufficiency-judge-user.md`; I read it after and it confirms the direction (endpoints-only anchors).
- **`injection_surface` = 0.6** — `{draftText}` interpolated bare after `DRAFT:` in all four judges, no delimiters or do-not-follow guards. Mild, but a draft could steer its own judge.

**Meta-audit** (state: `note-gate.ts` header + levels + builders — Jev judging our Jev questions):
- `levels_distinct` = 1.24/2 — "mostly distinct with neighbor blur." Acceptable; no action.
- **`noul_discipline` = 0.73** — something in there is a disguised magnitude. My prime suspect: `movesSuccessSignal` ("more *likely*" is a probability, not a fact) and the multi-condition `violatesFeedbackPreferences`. Worth a human re-read.
- **`missing_dimension` = quote-accuracy (0.57)** — the gate cannot catch a persona note that misquotes the draft. That's a concrete hole and a concrete new gate (below).

## Creative proposals, ordered by value

1. **Migrate the 4 generative judges → Jev Scores.** The level descriptions already exist in the user prompts — lift them into Score criteria. Kills the 0.88 fragility finding structurally (no JSON to parse), adds calibrated confidence, and the Target Fit cap over craft metrics becomes textbook composite scoring in code. At ~17k passes/dollar it's cheaper than the frontier calls they use now.
2. **New quote-accuracy gate on persona notes** (the 0.57 finding). Choice per note: quoted passage appears verbatim / paraphrased / absent — the citation-check cookbook pattern. Catches hallucinated evidence before the writer sees it.
3. **Dossier-check → per-field Noul cascade.** Seven yes/no questions over one state, no observation-array JSON to parse.
4. **Research-extract triage.** That 5KB system prompt runs per source; a Noul pre-filter ("does this source bear on the goal?") burns pennies to save dollars.
5. **`briefIsLoadBearing` → Jev Noul.** It's hand-tuned thresholds (`sufficiency < 0.4`, `NEEDS_WORK_BELOW`) guarding every downstream judgement — exactly the kind of semantic gate that drifts. Keep the heuristic as Tier 0, escalate disagreements.
6. **Eval harness judge → Jev Choice.** `evals/judge.ts` shells to Portkey/kimi for grounded/generic + good/poor — both are literally Choices. Calibrated, reproducible, no bearer-injection saga.
7. **Prompt CI gate.** Bottle this sweep: on any `prompts/**` or `note-gate` change, re-run the audit questions and fail on `output_fragility > 0.7` or a new weakest prompt. Prompt rot detector.
8. **Noul-discipline cleanup** in `note-gate.ts` — rephrase `movesSuccessSignal` as a fact ("does the note name a change that serves the success signal") or convert it to a Score.

Suggested order: 2 (new protection, small), 1 (kills the biggest measured problem), 7 (locks the gains). Say the word and I'll start with the quote-accuracy gate.

687: /**
688:  * Policy over a cached verdict. Pure and synchronous, like `viewRubricGrade`:
689:  * a writer moving a threshold re-renders from the verdict already in hand, and
690:  * no judgement is ever re-run to answer a slider.

692: export function noteAction(
693:   verdict: NoteVerdict,
694:   mode: NoteGateMode,
695:   attempt = 0,
696: ): NoteGateAction {
697:   if (mode === "annotate") {
698:     // Never hide what the writer explicitly pointed at.
699:     return { show: true, rewrite: null };
700:   }
701:   if (verdict.pass && verdict.rewriteKind === null) {
702:     return { show: true, rewrite: null };
703:   }
704:   if (attempt >= MAX_REWRITES) {
705:     // Out of retries. A vetoed note is withheld — it breaks something the
706:     // writer declared — but a merely mediocre one is still shown, because a
707:     // weak note the writer can ignore beats a silent room.
708:     return { show: !verdict.vetoed, rewrite: null };
709:   }
710:   return { show: !verdict.vetoed, rewrite: verdict.rewriteKind };
711: }
712: 
713: /**
714:  * Keep the best attempt, not the last one. A rewrite can come back worse, and
715:  * having paid for both there is no reason to show the worse one. Vetoed
716:  * attempts always lose to un-vetoed ones regardless of score.
717:  */
718: export function bestAttempt<T>(
719:   attempts: { note: T; verdict: NoteVerdict }[],
720: ): { note: T; verdict: NoteVerdict } | null {
721:   if (attempts.length === 0) return null;
722:   return attempts.reduce((best, a) => {
723:     if (best.verdict.vetoed !== a.verdict.vetoed) {
724:       return best.verdict.vetoed ? a : best;
725:     }
726:     return a.verdict.overall > best.verdict.overall ? a : best;
727:   });

content.text:
Both workstreams applied and verified. The headline finding first: **the note gate is dead code** — zero callers repo-wide. The best-designed Jev usage in the repo (tested, documented, 728 lines) never runs. I did not wire it into the live room unilaterally since that changes what writers see; say the word and I'll connect it at the note-production site.

## Sweep fixes

**Prompts** (9 files) — for the 0.88 fragility, 0.71 contradiction, 0.6 injection findings:
- All draft interpolations wrapped in `<draft>` tags + do-not-follow guard (target-fit, integrity, evidence, sufficiency, custom-criterion, dossier-check; missing-source already delimited, got the guard too).
- JSON escaping rule (`\"`, `\n`, single line) on every rationale/reason/claim field.
- Sufficiency scale gained 4/7 anchors; target-fit's "blind to craft" now exempts unintelligibility (blindness is about quality, not about being unable to tell what the piece is about).

**`note-gate.ts`** — for the 0.73 Noul-discipline and 0.57 missing-dimension findings:
- Removed `movesSuccessSignal`: asked every pass, consumed nowhere (verified full-repo). Its "informs but does not gate" test is gone with it.
- Added `misquotesPassage` Noul (unconditional — passage is always in state) with `quoteRisk`, `maxQuoteRisk: 0.75` veto, "Misquotes the passage" reason, and a new `"accuracy"` rewrite kind ("Quote the passage exactly as written…"). 31 gate tests pass, including 4 new ones.

Note: `parseJudgeOutput` already had brace-salvage + regex fallback, so the fragility fix belongs in the prompts (done), not the parser.

## Drift fixes

The preview was showing a stale room — generic Skeptic/Critic cast vs the real Mlle. Sceptique/Sœur Encourageante bouleversement, 4 renamed rubric criteria vs the 11-item spine, a hand-rolled dossier card, duplicated tabs/dateline/numerals. Now all shared by construction:
- New `board-tabs.ts` (`BOARD_TABS`) — editor route and preview import it; added the 5th tab the preview was missing all along.
- Preview cast derived from `PERSONAS` (names, roles, colors, marks) with in-voice notes rewritten per real editor; marginalia notes likewise.
- New `utils/editorial-format.ts` (`editorialDateline`, `folioNumeral`) — editor and preview import it.
- Preview drawer renders the real `ProjectBriefCard` with a canned brief (2 probes, 1 attachment).
- Rubric tab grades 4 real spine criteria (`thesis`, `structure`, `evidence`, `sufficiency`) with labels from `SPINE_CRITERIA`; `PanelId` replaces the duplicated tab type.
- New `workspace-drift.test.ts` (9 tests): cast ids/order/fields, tab shape, tour stops ⊆ real tabs/folios, rubric ids ⊆ spine, dateline + numeral cases.

## Verification

`tsc` clean, eslint clean (2 pre-existing image warnings), prettier applied (reverted 3 unrelated prompt reformats to keep the diff scoped), **1503 tests: 1463 pass, 39 skip, 1 fail** — the failure is `settings-select-wiring`, pre-existing working-tree state in `routes/settings/index.tsx` untouched by me. Storybook: 131 stories, no index errors. Tour behavior (hotspots, slip, auto-advance, sync) is unchanged — only its data got truer.

Accepted residuals: the manuscript stays static ProseMirror HTML (real TipTap needs IDB/models), and the masthead skips AccountMenu/zen — noted in the preview's docstring.

| Check | Result |

**On the 0.63:** I checked by hand. The only `successSignal` left in `note-gate.ts` is line 227 — the dossier brief field passed into gate *state*, not the removed verdict Noul — and the test file is fully clean. Removal is complete; Jev tripped on the homonym. Good reminder that a mid-range Noul deserves human reading, not blind action.

## De-drift verification

- `single_sourced` **0.87** — the sharing is real, not claimed.
- `guard_coverage` **1.1/2** — "partial with gaps" (0.81). Fair: the test pins every id with a source to pin to, but demo copy (sources, versions, notes text) has no source by nature. That's the honest ceiling for this technique.
- `biggest_residual_drift`: **canned-board-content (0.73)** — the tab panels show fixed demo data, not live results. Matches my accepted-residuals list; it's the next frontier if you want it (rendering real panels against canned stores — a bigger refactor than sharing data).

## Natural next targets, ranked by this review

1. **Dossier-check is now the weakest prompt.** Open-ended extraction (`observations[]` with free-text `current`/`suggested`) — the per-field Noul cascade from my earlier proposal would kill this structurally.
2. **`escaping_fixed` at 0.78**, not 0.95+. Something still itches — likely the system prompts (rules live only in user files) or the `claim`/`suggestedQuery` quoting in missing-source. A targeted re-read could pin it down.

62: function jsonObjectFrom(text: string): Record<string, unknown> | null {
63:   const fenced = text.match(/```(?:json)?\s*([\s\S]*?)```/i)?.[1];
64:   if (fenced) {

66:     if (parsed) return parsed;

69:   // Find the first balanced object that actually parses. This tolerates brief
70:   // prose before or after the JSON and ignores brace-shaped examples in that

72:   for (let start = 0; start < text.length; start++) {
73:     if (text[start] !== "{") continue;

75:     let inString = false;
76:     let escaped = false;

79:       if (inString) {

81:         else if (char === "\\") escaped = true;

109: export function parseDossierCheckResult(
110:   text: string,
111:   provider: string,
112:   answers: ProjectInterviewAnswers,
113: ): DossierCheckResult | null {
114:   const parsed = jsonObjectFrom(text);
115:   if (!parsed || !Array.isArray(parsed.observations)) return null;
116: 
117:   const seen = new Set<keyof ProjectInterviewAnswers>();
118:   const observations: DossierObservation[] = [];
119:   for (const item of parsed.observations) {
120:     if (!item || typeof item !== "object") continue;
121:     const record = item as Record<string, unknown>;
122:     const field = stringValue(record.field);
123:     if (!DOSSIER_FIELD_SET.has(field)) continue;
124:     const typedField = field as keyof ProjectInterviewAnswers;
125:     if (seen.has(typedField)) continue;
126: 
127:     const suggested = stringValue(record.suggested);
128:     const reason = stringValue(record.reason);
129:     // A report without an actionable replacement or an explanation cannot be
130:     // meaningfully applied or assessed by the writer.
131:     if (!suggested || !reason) continue;
132: 
133:     observations.push({
134:       field: typedField,
135:       current: stringValue(record.current) || answers[typedField],
136:       suggested,
137:       reason,
138:     });
139:     seen.add(typedField);
140:   }

142:   return {
143:     observations: observations.slice(0, DOSSIER_FIELDS.length),

1: /**
2:  * The background room — the editors read as you write.
3:  *
4:  * Convening is expensive and deliberate: five model calls over the whole
5:  * manuscript, triggered by a button. That is the right shape for "tell me what
6:  * you think", and the wrong shape for "keep up with me". So this module runs
7:  * the same five editors on a much narrower brief — only the material that is
8:  * new since they last looked, plus a digest of how the draft has been moving —
9:  * on a trigger tuned to catch the moment a writer finishes a thought.
10:  *
11:  * The trigger has two conditions, and both must hold:
12:  *
13:  *   1. At least {@link WORD_DELTA_THRESHOLD} net new words since the last pass.
14:  *      Fiddling with a sentence is not something to interrupt over.
15:  *   2. Then {@link IDLE_MS} of no typing. This is an *idle* timer, not a
16:  *      debounce window: every keystroke pushes it back, so the room waits
17:  *      until the writer has actually stopped rather than firing mid-paragraph.
18:  *
19:  * On top of that sit two spend guards — a hard floor between passes and a
20:  * per-session cap — because this runs without the writer asking, and anything
21:  * that spends their money unasked should be conservative by construction.
22:  *
23:  * Structurally this mirrors `background-research.ts`, which already solved the
24:  * same watcher problem for the Apparatus.
25:  */
26: 
27: import type { ConvexClient } from "convex/browser";
28: import { api } from "../../convex/_generated/api";
29: import { toAgentPersona } from "../../convex/agentPrompts";
30: import type { Persona, PersonaFeedback, ProjectBrief } from "../types";
31: import {
32:   MIN_EDITOR_WORDS,
33:   WORDS_PER_FOLIO,
34:   countWords,
35: } from "./draft-thresholds";
36: import {
37:   appendTrajectory,
38:   diffParagraphs,
39:   entryFromDiff,
40:   loadTrajectory,
41:   trajectoryDigest,
42: } from "./draft-trajectory";
43: import { hasConfiguredAiProvider, runClientAgent } from "./ai-client";
44: import { getCachedAiSettings } from "./ai-orchestrator";
45: import { loadWriterSettingsFromIdb } from "./idb";
46: import { savePersonaNoteLocally } from "./convex-sync";
47: import { reportApplicationDiagnostic } from "./application-diagnostics";
48: 
49: /** Wait for another substantive folio before automatically reading again. */
50: export const WORD_DELTA_THRESHOLD = WORDS_PER_FOLIO;
51: 
52: /** Quiet time required after that threshold is crossed. */
53: export const IDLE_MS = 120_000;
54: 
55: /**
56:  * Hard floor between passes, independent of how much gets written. Protects
57:  * against a fast writer triggering back-to-back five-call passes, and keeps us
58:  * well inside the server's `agentRoom` rate limit of 6/min.
59:  */
60: export const MIN_INTERVAL_MS = 5 * 60_000;
61: 
62: /** Passes allowed per session, so a long day can't run away with spend. */
63: export const MAX_PASSES_PER_SESSION = 8;
64: 
65: export type BackgroundRoomStatus =
66:   | "off"
67:   | "idle"
68:   | "armed"
69:   | "reading"
70:   | "error";
71: 
72: export interface BackgroundRoomSnapshot {
73:   status: BackgroundRoomStatus;
74:   /** Net new words accumulated since the last pass. */
75:   pendingWords: number;
76:   passesThisSession: number;
77:   lastPassAt: number;
78:   lastNoteCount: number;
79:   folioId: string | null;
80:   error?: string;
81: }
82: 
83: interface RoomState {
84:   status: BackgroundRoomStatus;
85:   pendingWords: number;
86:   passesThisSession: number;
87:   lastPassAt: number;
88:   lastNoteCount: number;
89:   error?: string;
90: }
91: 
92: const state: RoomState = {
93:   status: "off",
94:   pendingWords: 0,
95:   passesThisSession: 0,
96:   lastPassAt: 0,
97:   lastNoteCount: 0,
98: };
99: 
100: let idleTimer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | null = null;
101: let activeClient: ConvexClient | null = null;
102: let activeBrief: ProjectBrief | null = null;
103: let activeFolioId: string | null = null;
104: let activePersonas: Persona[] = [];
105: let enabled = false;
106: /** Text as of the last completed pass — the baseline for "what is new". */
107: let lastReadText = "";
108: /** Most recent draft text seen, so the idle timer has something to work on. */
109: let latestText = "";
110: let running = false;
111: 
112: export function snapshot(): BackgroundRoomSnapshot {
113:   return {
114:     status: state.status,
115:     pendingWords: state.pendingWords,
116:     passesThisSession: state.passesThisSession,
117:     lastPassAt: state.lastPassAt,
118:     lastNoteCount: state.lastNoteCount,
119:     folioId: activeFolioId,
120:     error: state.error,
121:   };
122: }
123: 
124: function notify(): void {
125:   if (typeof window === "undefined") return;
126:   if (typeof window.dispatchEvent !== "function") return;
127:   window.dispatchEvent(
128:     new CustomEvent("twyne:background-room", { detail: snapshot() }),
129:   );
130: }
131: 
132: function setStatus(status: BackgroundRoomStatus, error?: string): void {
133:   state.status = status;
134:   state.error = error;
135:   notify();
136: }
137: 
138: function clearIdleTimer(): void {
139:   if (idleTimer) {
140:     clearTimeout(idleTimer);
141:     idleTimer = null;
142:   }
143: }
144: 
145: /**
146:  * Configure the watcher. Safe to call repeatedly — the latest arguments win,
147:  * which is what the editor route needs when the writer switches folio.
148:  */
149: export function startBackgroundRoom(args: {
150:   /** Undefined when Qwik has not yet resumed the client — treated as absent. */
151:   client: ConvexClient | null | undefined;
152:   brief: ProjectBrief | null;
153:   folioId: string | null;
154:   personas: Persona[];
155:   enabled: boolean;
156:   /** Current draft text, used as the baseline so existing prose isn't "new". */
157:   baselineText?: string;
158: }): void {
159:   const folioChanged = args.folioId !== activeFolioId;
160:   activeClient = args.client ?? null;
161:   activeBrief = args.brief;
162:   activeFolioId = args.folioId;
163:   activePersonas = args.personas;
164:   enabled = args.enabled;
165: 
166:   if (folioChanged) {
167:     // A new folio is a new conversation: everything already on the page has
168:     // been "read" as far as the background room is concerned, so the writer
169:     // isn't ambushed by five notes on prose they wrote last week.
170:     lastReadText = args.baselineText ?? "";
171:     latestText = lastReadText;
172:     state.pendingWords = 0;
173:     clearIdleTimer();
174:   } else if (args.baselineText !== undefined && !lastReadText) {
175:     lastReadText = args.baselineText;
176:     latestText = args.baselineText;
177:   }
178: 
179:   setStatus(enabled ? "idle" : "off");
180: }
181: 
182: /**
183:  * Turn the watcher on or off without tearing down its baseline, so flipping
184:  * the setting twice does not make the whole draft look new.
185:  */
186: export function setBackgroundRoomEnabled(next: boolean): void {
187:   if (enabled === next) return;
188:   enabled = next;
189:   if (!next) {
190:     clearIdleTimer();
191:     setStatus("off");
192:     return;
193:   }
194:   setStatus("idle");
195:   // Re-evaluate against the text we already have, so switching it back on
196:   // mid-session picks up work done while it was off rather than waiting for
197:   // the next keystroke.
198:   if (latestText) onDraftChanged(latestText);
199: }
200: 
201: export function stopBackgroundRoom(): void {
202:   clearIdleTimer();
203:   enabled = false;
204:   activeClient = null;
205:   activeFolioId = null;
206:   activePersonas = [];
207:   lastReadText = "";
208:   latestText = "";
209:   state.pendingWords = 0;
210:   state.status = "off";
211: }
212: 
213: /**
214:  * The writer convened the room explicitly, so everything currently on the page
215:  * has now been read. Rebaselines from the watcher's own `latestText` rather
216:  * than from a caller-supplied string: the caller reads the draft through a
217:  * different path (`editor.getText()`) than the watcher does
218:  * (`paragraphTextFromHtml`), and the two must not be allowed to disagree about
219:  * where paragraphs begin — a mis-aligned baseline would make the next diff
220:  * report the whole document as new.
221:  */
222: export function noteExplicitConvene(): void {
223:   lastReadText = latestText;
224:   state.pendingWords = 0;
225:   state.lastPassAt = Date.now();
226:   clearIdleTimer();
227:   setStatus(enabled ? "idle" : "off");
228: }
229: 
230: /**
231:  * Notify the watcher that the draft changed. Cheap enough to call on every
232:  * keystroke: it does a word count and resets a timer.
233:  */
234: export function onDraftChanged(draftText: string): void {
235:   if (!enabled || !activeFolioId) return;
236:   latestText = draftText;
237: 
238:   const delta = countWords(draftText) - countWords(lastReadText);
239:   state.pendingWords = delta;
240: 
241:   if (delta < WORD_DELTA_THRESHOLD) {
242:     // Below the threshold there is nothing to wait for; drop any armed timer
243:     // so a writer who deletes back down doesn't get a pass on stale material.
244:     if (state.status === "armed") {
245:       clearIdleTimer();
246:       setStatus("idle");
247:     }
248:     return;
249:   }
250: 
251:   // Armed: wait for the writer to stop. Every keystroke pushes this back.
252:   clearIdleTimer();
253:   if (state.status !== "armed") setStatus("armed");
254:   idleTimer = setTimeout(() => {
255:     idleTimer = null;
256:     void runPass();
257:   }, IDLE_MS);
258: }
259: 
260: /** Reasons a pass may be declined, for tests and diagnostics. */
261: export type SkipReason =
262:   | "disabled"
263:   | "no-folio"
264:   | "already-running"
265:   | "session-cap"
266:   | "too-soon"
267:   | "too-short"
268:   | "no-new-material"
269:   | "no-provider";
270: 
271: export function whyNotReady(now: number = Date.now()): SkipReason | null {
272:   if (!enabled) return "disabled";
273:   if (!activeFolioId) return "no-folio";
274:   if (running) return "already-running";
275:   if (state.passesThisSession >= MAX_PASSES_PER_SESSION) return "session-cap";
276:   if (state.lastPassAt > 0 && now - state.lastPassAt < MIN_INTERVAL_MS) {
277:     return "too-soon";
278:   }
279:   if (countWords(latestText) < MIN_EDITOR_WORDS) return "too-short";
280:   return null;
281: }
282: 
283: /**
284:  * Run a pass now, bypassing the idle wait but not the spend guards. Returns
285:  * the notes produced, or an empty array when the pass was declined.
286:  */
287: export async function runPass(): Promise<PersonaFeedback[]> {
288:   const blocked = whyNotReady();
289:   if (blocked) {
290:     if (blocked !== "already-running") setStatus(enabled ? "idle" : "off");
291:     return [];
292:   }
293: 
294:   const draftText = latestText;
295:   const diff = diffParagraphs(lastReadText, draftText);
296:   if (diff.added.length === 0) {
297:     // Words moved but no paragraph is genuinely new — nothing to read.
298:     state.pendingWords = 0;
299:     setStatus("idle");
300:     return [];
301:   }
302: 
303:   running = true;
304:   setStatus("reading");
305:   const folioId = activeFolioId!;
306: 
307:   try {
308:     // Record the movement before the call, so the digest the editors receive
309:     // includes the material they are about to read.
310:     const entry = entryFromDiff(diff);
311:     const history = entry
312:       ? await appendTrajectory(folioId, entry)
313:       : await loadTrajectory(folioId);
314:     const digest = trajectoryDigest(history);
315:     const newMaterial = diff.added.join("\n\n");
316: 
317:     const responses = await conveneQuietly({
318:       draftText,
319:       newMaterial,
320:       trajectory: digest,
321:     });
322:     if (responses.length === 0) {
323:       setStatus("idle");
324:       return [];
325:     }
326: 
327:     const timestamp = Date.now();
328:     const notes: PersonaFeedback[] = [];
329:     for (const r of responses) {
330:       const persona = activePersonas.find((p) => p.id === r.personaId);
331:       if (!persona || !r.text.trim()) continue;
332:       const note: PersonaFeedback = {
333:         folioId: activeFolioId!,
334:         personaId: r.personaId,
335:         personaName: persona.name,
336:         personaColor: persona.color,
337:         feedback: r.text,
338:         timestamp,
339:         type: r.type,
340:         anchor: r.anchor,
341:         noteId: `bg-${r.personaId}-${timestamp}`,
342:         origin: "background",
343:       };
344:       notes.push(note);
345:       await savePersonaNoteLocally(note, activeBrief, activeFolioId!);
346:     }
347: 
348:     lastReadText = draftText;
349:     state.pendingWords = 0;
350:     state.lastPassAt = timestamp;
351:     state.passesThisSession += 1;
352:     state.lastNoteCount = notes.length;
353: 
354:     if (typeof window !== "undefined" && notes.length > 0) {
355:       window.dispatchEvent(
356:         new CustomEvent("twyne:background-room-notes", { detail: notes }),
357:       );
358:     }
359:     setStatus("idle");
360:     return notes;
361:   } catch (err) {
362:     reportApplicationDiagnostic("twyne:background-room:pass", err, {
363:       feature: "background-room",
364:       operation: "pass",
365:     });
366:     setStatus("error", (err as Error)?.message);
367:     return [];
368:   } finally {
369:     running = false;

371: }

373: interface QuietResponse {

1: import type { RequestHandler } from "@qwik.dev/router";
2: 
3: /**
4:  * Stable per-platform desktop download links.
5:  *
6:  * Served at `/download/macos`, `/download/windows`, `/download/linux`. CI
7:  * publishes versioned assets (e.g. `twyne-desktop-macos-1.4.2.tar.gz`) to the
8:  * latest GitHub release, so there is no fixed file URL to hardcode. This
9:  * endpoint asks the GitHub API for the latest release, finds the asset whose
10:  * name starts with `twyne-desktop-<platform>`, and 302-redirects to it.
11:  *
12:  * On any miss (unknown platform, no matching asset, API failure) it falls back
13:  * to our own downloads page rather than erroring or bouncing visitors out to
14:  * GitHub, so a button always lands somewhere useful.
15:  */
16: 
17: const REPO = "Diogenesoftoronto/twyne";
18: const LATEST_API = `https://api.github.com/repos/${REPO}/releases/latest`;
19: /** Fallback when no matching asset can be resolved — keep visitors on our own site. */
20: const DOWNLOADS_PAGE = "/downloads/";
21: 
22: /** Normalise common aliases to the asset-name platform token. */
23: const PLATFORM_ALIASES: Record<string, "macos" | "windows" | "linux"> = {
24:   macos: "macos",
25:   mac: "macos",
26:   osx: "macos",
27:   darwin: "macos",
28:   apple: "macos",
29:   windows: "windows",
30:   win: "windows",
31:   win64: "windows",
32:   linux: "linux",
33: };
34: 
35: interface GitHubAsset {
36:   name: string;
37:   browser_download_url: string;
38: }
39: 
40: export const onGet: RequestHandler = async ({ params, redirect, headers }) => {
41:   // Let CDNs/browsers cache the redirect briefly so we don't hammer GitHub's
42:   // unauthenticated rate limit (60 req/hr) on every button click.
43:   headers.set("Cache-Control", "public, max-age=900, s-maxage=900");
44: 
45:   const platform = PLATFORM_ALIASES[(params.platform ?? "").toLowerCase()];
46: 
47:   // Resolve the asset URL first; only throw the redirect once, afterwards, so
48:   // Qwik City's thrown-redirect control flow isn't caught by our own try/catch.
49:   let target = DOWNLOADS_PAGE;
50:   if (platform) {
51:     try {
52:       const res = await fetch(LATEST_API, {
53:         headers: {
54:           Accept: "application/vnd.github+json",
55:           "User-Agent": "twyne-download-redirect",
56:         },
57:       });
58:       if (res.ok) {
59:         const release = (await res.json()) as { assets?: GitHubAsset[] };
60:         const prefix = `twyne-desktop-${platform}`;
61:         const asset = release.assets?.find((a) => a.name.startsWith(prefix));
62:         if (asset) {
63:           target = asset.browser_download_url;
64:         }
65:       }
66:     } catch {
67:       // Network/parse failure — fall back to the downloads page below.
68:     }
69:   }
70: 
71:   throw redirect(302, target);
72: };

<sub>2026-08-27</sub>

-  *(minor)*
  Twyne 0.18 gives every writer a private, local-first desk for understanding
  their work, their editorial activity, and the cost of AI assistance.

  **My Desk turns usage into a writing history.** A new responsive workspace
  brings together active days, current folios, editorial actions, recent work,
  deterministic writing patterns, and accessible charts. Signed-out writers keep
  the full experience on this device; signed-in writers can synchronize it across

  **AI cost is legible without pretending estimates are bills.** The ledger

  unknown cost, token dimensions, providers, models, features, and folios. Writers
  can inspect the methodology, export JSON or CSV, clear local history, and delete
  synchronized records.

  **Public profiles remain private by default.** Writers can explicitly share a
  small set of writing statistics while tokens, cost, models, private folios, and

  analytics, provider diagnostics, and application error recovery are also more

content.text:
All verified. What's changed:

**First-party downloads** — nobody leaves the site anymore:
- `/download/macos|windows|linux` now **streams the bytes** through twyne.love (`Content-Disposition: attachment`, proper filename) instead of 302ing to `github.com` file URLs. Verified live: `/download/macos` → 200 `application/gzip`, `twyne-desktop-macos-v0.19.1.tar.gz`, from our domain. GitHub API resolution is cached 15 min, optional `GITHUB_TOKEN` raises the ceiling, misses still fall back to our own downloads page.
- **Release notes live on the page now** — parsed at build time from the repo's `CHANGELOG.md` (new tested `utils/changelog.ts`; top 3 releases with dates + highlights). The "releases page on GitHub" link is gone, as is the "published to GitHub" copy.
- Landing page CTAs ("Desktop app" nav, "Download Twyne for desktop") are internal `Link`s to `/downloads/`; download buttons download in place instead of opening blank tabs. Zero `github.com` links remain anywhere in the download flow.

**Real reicon.dev icons** — one honest finding first: reicon ships no OS brand logos (2674 icons, all generic — brand marks would be trademark-sensitive). So I rendered candidates to PNG, eyeballed them, and picked the closest true stock:
- macOS → `Command` (actual ⌘ loop, perfect)
- Windows → `Grid2` (pane grid nodding at the mark)
- Linux → `BrowserTerminal` (`>_` terminal)
- iOS → `Iphone` (notched phone)
- Android → `Devices` (generic device, distinct from iPhone)

Registered all five in `icon-system.ts` (generic names per registry convention), added them to the icon catalogue story, and swapped the downloads glyphs (`⌘⊞⌂◈▲`) for `<Icon size={26}>` in ink color.

Verification: tsc clean, eslint clean (only pre-existing warnings), full suite 1466 pass with only the pre-existing settings failure, 131 stories no errors, plus live endpoint checks above.
